blocks.text: Use case diagrams are a fundamental part of UML used to show the ways in which users, called actors, interact with a system. They give a visual view of the system's functionality from the user's perspective, helping to identify the requirements and the interactions between users and the system.

blocks.title: Use case
blocks.text: A use case is a description of a set of interactions between a user (actor) and a system to achieve a specific goal. Each use case represents a complete workflow from the user's perspective, detailing the steps involved in accomplishing a particular task.

items: Capturing functional requirements: identifying and documenting what the system must do.
Understanding user interactions: how different users will use the system.
Planning and testing: planning development and designing test cases to check the system's functions.
Identify actors: the types of users, people or other systems, who will interact with the system.
Define goals: what each actor needs to accomplish with the system.
Outline interactions: describe the interactions that achieve these goals; each one with a significant outcome is a possible use case.
Validate use cases: review them with stakeholders to check they capture the required functions and interactions.

blocks.text: In Figure 1.9 a library system's use case diagram shows two actors, a librarian and a student, both connected to the use cases Borrow book and Return book inside the system boundary. In the class activity on an online shopping platform, the actors are the customer, the administrator and the delivery personnel, and the use cases are browse products, add items to cart, make purchase, manage product listings, process orders, handle customer inquiries and update delivery status.

blocks.alt: A tall rounded box titled Simple Use case diagram holds two ovals, Borrow book and Return book. Outside the box, the actor Librarian stands on the left and the actor Student on the right; each is joined by a line to both ovals.
